title: JSON, Optional Chaining, and Deep Copies
summary: Turn data into JSON text and back, read nested data safely with ?. and ??, and copy nested data without sharing it.
intro: JSON is the text format that programs use to save and send data. Here you turn objects into JSON text and back, read nested data that may be missing without crashing, and copy nested data so a change to the copy never leaks into the original.

steps.title: JSON.stringify

example.title: Serialize a user
example.prompt: Turn a user object into compact and pretty JSON, and convert a Map and a BigInt before serializing them.
example.explanation: The compact line drops `nickname` (undefined) and `greet` (a function), and `score` (NaN) becomes `null`. With `null, 2` the same data spreads over lines with 2 spaces per level. The Map prints as `{}` until `Object.fromEntries` turns it into a plain object. The BigInt goes through `String()` first, so it is saved as text and nothing throws.

practice.title: Serialize an order
hints: `coupon` is undefined, so it disappears, and `Infinity` becomes `null`.
The third argument of `JSON.stringify` sets the indentation. Pass `null` as the second.
A Set has to become an array before JSON can show its values. Spread syntax does that.

steps.title: JSON.parse
steps.body:
`JSON.parse(text)` reads JSON text and builds real objects and arrays. Numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays, and nested objects come back with their types, so you can do math and loops on them right away.

```javascript
const data = JSON.parse('{"n":5,"ok":true,"list":[1,2]}');
console.log(data.n + 1);       // 6
console.log(data.list.length); // 2
```

JSON is stricter than JavaScript: keys and strings must use double quotes, and trailing commas are not allowed. That is why JSON text written in code sits in a single-quoted string, so its double quotes need no escaping.

Invalid JSON such as `{name: "Ada"}` or `{'a': 1}` makes `JSON.parse` throw a SyntaxError. You learn to catch errors later, so every JSON string here is valid.

A round trip, `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))`, gives back new objects with the same data, as long as the data only holds JSON types. This is how programs save data and load it again.

example.title: Load a team
example.prompt: Parse a team from JSON, read its fields and members, add a member, and serialize again.
example.output:
Team: Rockets
Types: number, boolean
Coach: null
Ada: lead
Linus: dev
Total commits: 65
{"name":"Grace","role":"tester","commits":0}
Copy has 3 members
example.explanation: After `JSON.parse`, `founded` is a real number, `active` a real boolean, and `coach` is `null`, not the text `"null"`. `members` is an ordinary array of objects, so `for...of` and `reduce` work on it. Pushing a new object changes the parsed data, and `JSON.stringify` turns the last member back into text. The round trip builds a separate copy that still has all 3 members.

practice.title: Weather report
practice.prompt:
Parse a weather report and summarize it.

1. Parse `text` into `report` with `JSON.parse`.
2. Print `City: ` followed by the city.
3. Print `Average high: ` followed by the average of the `high` values to 1 decimal place.
4. Find the day with the highest `high` and print it with `JSON.stringify`. If days tie, keep the first one.

Expected output:

```text
City: Lisbon
Average high: 28.0
{"day":"Wed","high":31.5,"rain":false}
```
hints: `report.days` is an ordinary array of objects after parsing.
Sum with `reduce`, divide by `report.days.length`, then call `toFixed(1)`.
Find the hottest day with `reduce` too: start from the first day and keep whichever of the two has the bigger `high`.

steps.title: Optional chaining with ?.

example.title: Cities and tags
example.prompt: Print each user's city and first tag, using defaults when parts are missing.
example.output:
Ada: London, admin
Linus: unknown, none
Grace: unknown, none
nobody: undefined
OK
no lower
example.explanation: Linus has no `address`, so `user.address?.city` is `undefined` and `??` picks `"unknown"`. Grace has an address, but its city is `null`, which `??` also replaces. `tags?.[0]` handles both an empty array (no first item) and `null` tags. `nobody?.address.city` stops at `nobody`, so it prints `undefined` instead of throwing. `format.lower` does not exist, so `?.()` skips the call and `??` supplies the text.

practice.title: Shipping carriers
practice.prompt:
Report each order's carrier and first item, even when parts of the order are missing.

1. Complete `carrierOf(order)` so it returns `order.shipping?.tracking?.carrier`, or `"pending"` when that is missing.
2. Complete `firstItem(order)` so it returns the first entry of `order.items`, or `"none"` when there is none.
3. The loop already prints `id: carrier, item` for each order.
4. Print `labels.short?.(101)`, or `no short` if it is missing.
5. Print `labels.long?.(101)`, or `no long` if it is missing.

Expected output:

```text
101: UPS, pen
102: pending, none
103: pending, none
104: DHL, ink
#101
no long
```

tests.output:
101: UPS, pen
102: pending, none
103: pending, none
104: DHL, ink
#101
no long

hints: Order 102 has no `shipping` and order 103 has no `tracking`, so both steps need `?.`. Order 102 also has no `items`, and order 103 has an empty list.
End each chain with `??` and its fallback text. For `items`, put `?.` before the brackets, as `firstTag` does in the example.
Call a method that may not exist with `?.` placed between its name and the parentheses, then add `??` with the fallback text.

steps.title: Deep copies

example.title: Copy settings
example.prompt: Copy nested settings with spread and with structuredClone, change each copy, and see what reaches the original. Then compare a JSON copy with a clone, and clone a class instance.
example.output:
theme: dark
fontSize: 18
tabs: main.js
spread shares editor: true
clone shares editor: false
json: {"lang":"en","recent":{}}, has draft: false
clone recent a.js: true, has draft: true
copy: {"x":3,"y":4}, describe: undefined
example.explanation: The spread copy has its own `theme`, so `"light"` stays in the copy. But `editor` is shared, so the font size change shows in `settings`. The clone has its own `editor` and `tabs`, so pushing `"util.js"` leaves the original alone. The JSON copy turns the Set into `{}` and drops `draft`, while `structuredClone` keeps a real Set and the `undefined` key. Cloning `Point` keeps `x` and `y` but loses the `describe` method, so its type is `undefined`.

practice.title: Copy a gradebook
practice.prompt:
Copy a gradebook two ways and check what reaches the original.

1. Copy `gradebook` with `Object.assign({}, gradebook)` into `shallow` and push `100` to `shallow.ada`.
2. Copy `gradebook` with `structuredClone` into `deep` and push `60` to `deep.linus`.
3. Print `ada: ` and `linus: ` with the lengths of the original's arrays.
4. Print `assign shares ada: ` with whether `shallow.ada === gradebook.ada`, then `clone shares linus: ` with whether `deep.linus === gradebook.linus`.
5. Copy `meta` with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(meta))` into `jsonCopy` and with `structuredClone` into `cloned`.
6. On one line, print `json: `, then `JSON.stringify(jsonCopy)`, then `, has term: `, then whether `"term" in jsonCopy`.
7. On one line, print `clone seen ada: `, then whether `cloned.seen.has("ada")`, then `, has term: `, then whether `"term" in cloned`.

Expected output:

```text
ada: 3
linus: 1
assign shares ada: true
clone shares linus: false
json: {"owner":"kim","seen":{}}, has term: false
clone seen ada: true, has term: true
```

tests.output:
ada: 3
linus: 1
assign shares ada: true
clone shares linus: false
json: {"owner":"kim","seen":{}}, has term: false
clone seen ada: true, has term: true

hints: `Object.assign` works like spread, so `shallow.ada` is the same array as `gradebook.ada`.
`structuredClone` gives `deep` its own arrays, so pushing to `deep.linus` leaves the original at 1 grade.
Check the JSON copy and the clone the same way the example checks `prefs`.

recap:
- `JSON.stringify(value)` makes compact JSON text, and `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)` pretty-prints it.
- `undefined` values and functions are skipped, `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`, and a Map or Set becomes `{}`.
- Convert first: `Object.fromEntries(map)`, `[...set]`, and `String(big)` for a BigInt, which would otherwise throw a TypeError.
- `JSON.parse(text)` gives back numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays, and nested objects. JSON needs double-quoted keys and strings.
- `obj?.prop`, `arr?.[0]`, and `obj.method?.()` give `undefined` instead of throwing, and `?? fallback` supplies a default.
- Spread and `Object.assign` copy only the top level. `structuredClone(value)` copies nested data too, including Map and Set.
- A cloned class instance is a plain object without methods or private fields. `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` drops `undefined` and breaks Map and Set.
